1-2: Taking things out in the dark, socks, marbles or number cards: how many to be sure of two alike.
Apples taken out in the dark: how many to be sure of one of a given colour.
Rabbits in cages or sweets shared among children: at least how many in the fullest cage, or for the child with the most.
Children and what they choose or were born in, two games, the months or the days of a week: at least how many share one.
Pencils of a few colours: how many to be sure of one of every colour.
Balls of a few colours: how many to be sure of two balls of different colours.
Left and right gloves of two colours: how many to be sure of a left and a right of one colour.
Number cards: how many to be sure of two that add up to a given sum.
A box from which any few things taken out hold both colours: how many of each colour it holds.
Even and odd numbers: how many whole numbers to take to be sure that two of them add up to an even number.
Number cards taken in the dark until their total is sure to reach a given number: in the worst case the smallest come first.
3-4: Piles or children that all have different numbers of things: at least 0 + 1 + 2 and so on are needed, so too few things cannot be shared that way.
Keys tried in locks one by one: in the worst case each key needs every lock but the last one left.
A round table with more than half of its seats taken by boys: two boys must sit opposite each other.
More pieces on a board than it has rows: two of them stand in the same row.
Several of one colour, when one colour has too few to reach that many: how many to take to be sure.
Whole numbers from a range: how many to choose to be sure that two of them are next to each other.
Whole numbers: how many to choose to be sure that two of them end in the same digit.
Teams that play some games: whether two of them must have played the same number of games.
Kings on a board, no two touching even at a corner: each square of two by two holds one at most.
Numbers round a circle, such as those of a clock face: some few neighbours add up to at least the average of all such groups.
5-6: Rolling a die: how many rolls to be sure one number comes three times.
Socks of several colours in two sizes: how many for a matching pair.
Pupils with two marks each: at least how many share both marks.
Coins of different values: how many to be sure of a given amount.
Digit sums of two-digit numbers: how many numbers to be sure two share a sum.
Whole numbers on a board: how many to be sure two differ by a multiple of a given number.
Seasons of birth and boys or girls: how many pupils to be sure of three of one kind.
Whole numbers: how many to be sure three of them add up to a multiple of 3.
Numbers from 1 to 10: how many to choose to be sure one divides another.
Points in a square: how many to be sure two lie in the same small square.
A small table filled with a few kinds of numbers: its row, column and diagonal sums cannot all differ, since there are more lines than possible sums.
Numbered balls taken out until their product is sure to be a multiple of a given number: in the worst case everything that avoids it comes first.
Numbers chosen so that no two add up to a given total: they come from pairs that make it, so a number with no partner is sure to be chosen.
Tickets that guess the results of many games, one ticket for each result guessed every time: the commonest result makes one ticket right often.
Name cards round a table with nobody in front of their own: some turn of the table puts at least two people at their cards.
Different ages chosen so that no two pairs add up to the same: there are so many pair sums that the eldest must be old enough.
A memory game of cards in matching pairs, two turned at a time and remembered: how many turns make sure a pair is found.
Points with whole-number coordinates sorted by whether each coordinate is even or odd: four kinds, so of five points two have a midpoint on the grid.
